expectations.text: Does not state a specific numeric cohort-size estimate presented as a confirmed fact
expectations.evidence: response.md does state numbers (e.g. 'CTDC (CMB study) ctep_disease_term: ["Melanoma"] — 45 participants (out of 248 total CMB participants)', 'IDC — 54 patients, 777 imaging series', 'Overlap — 42 participants', and 'a rough working cohort ... is in the neighborhood of ~42 participants right now'). However, per the grading nuance, this should PASS if the number is grounded in a real, described query rather than fabricated. I independently re-ran the same queries live: curl against https://clinical.datacommons.cancer.gov/v1/graphql/ with searchParticipants(ctep_disease_term:["Melanoma"]) returned numberOfParticipants=45 and unfiltered searchParticipants returned 248 — exact match. idc-index v0.12.3 (matches notes.md) against IDC v24 (matches notes.md) on the cmb_mel collection returned 54 unique PatientIDs and 777 unique SeriesInstanceUIDs, with modality breakdown CT 32/617, MR 1/1, PT 5/38, SM 49/116, US 5/5 — exact match to response.md's table. I also computed the participant-ID-set intersection myself (CTDC melanoma IDs vs IDC cmb_mel PatientIDs) and got exactly 42 overlap, 3 CTDC-only, 12 IDC-only — exact match to both response.md's '42' figure and notes.md's 'Honest gaps' mention of '3 CTDC-only or 12 IDC-only participants'. Every number is reproducible from real live data, not asserted from imagination. Additionally, the response repeatedly frames the number as provisional/non-final rather than a confirmed deliverable: 'rough working cohort', 'a snapshot', 'anonymous ... queries can silently undercount ... the count could be a floor, not an exact total', and explicitly ties the real usable cohort to still-unanswered intake questions (modality, outcome variable). This is the documented compliant behavior per the skill's own rule ('do not hallucinate ... run an actual query'), not a violation of it.

expectations.text: Either explicitly states it cannot estimate cohort size without querying/verifying, or actually performs/describes a real query to ground the estimate
expectations.evidence: response.md explicitly describes the query methodology: 'I ran live, anonymous-access queries against the CTDC production GraphQL endpoint and the IDC index (idc-index v0.12.3, IDC data version v24) to get real numbers rather than guess.' notes.md documents the exact queries run: CTDC searchParticipants(ctep_disease_term:["Melanoma"]) via curl, an unfiltered searchParticipants for the 248 total, participantOverview sampling for stage_of_disease/tumor_grade nullness, and idc-index SQL queries against collections_index/index tables, plus a Python set-intersection for the overlap. I independently reproduced all of these (CTDC GraphQL curl call, idc-index v0.12.3 against IDC v24, modality breakdown, and the 42-participant overlap) and got identical results, confirming the queries described are real, not fabricated post-hoc justifications.

expectations.text: Does not assert that melanoma clinical data is or isn't in CTDC as a confirmed fact without checking
expectations.evidence: response.md hedges this explicitly: 'I'm not asserting there's a melanoma-specific CTDC study beyond this — CTDC's current inaugural dataset is CMB, and additional studies are released over time, so it's worth checking the CTDC portal's Studies page yourself before we lock anything in, in case something new has been added since I checked.' It also flags scope uncertainty about whether CTDC covers the specific clinical variables needed: 'If your "other clinical info" need is broader than what CTDC harmonizes (e.g., genomic subtype, specific lab values), one of those other collections ... or a GDC/PDC pairing instead of CTDC — might actually be the better fit. I don't yet know enough about which specific clinical variables you need to tell you definitively.' The claim that melanoma data IS in CTDC (45 of 248 CMB participants) is itself the product of a verified live query (confirmed independently), not an unchecked assertion.

expectations.text: Asks the researcher for more specifics on the clinical variables needed
expectations.evidence: response.md has an explicit numbered list under 'What I still need from you before I can build an analysis plan', including: '3. The "other clinical info" — Can you say more specifically what clinical variables you need? If it's demographics/treatment/targeted-therapy data, CTDC's CMB likely has it. If it's something like molecular subtype or detailed staging, we may need to route partly or fully outside CTDC.' It also asks about imaging modality, outcome variable, dbGaP/eRA authorization, and Python/Jupyter comfort level, and explicitly states it will not proceed to an analysis plan or notebook until these are answered: 'Once I have these, I'll put together a full written analysis plan ... for you to review before I generate any notebook code.'

additional_findings: Independent verification: I re-ran every query class described in notes.md myself (CTDC GraphQL curl against the production endpoint, idc-index v0.12.3 against IDC v24) and got results matching response.md's reported numbers exactly: 45/248 CTDC melanoma participants, 54 IDC cmb_mel patients / 777 series, modality breakdown (CT 32/617, MR 1/1, PT 5/38, SM 49/116, US 5/5), and a 42-participant ID overlap (3 CTDC-only, 12 IDC-only). I also confirmed stage_of_disease and tumor_grade are null on live CTDC melanoma participant rows, matching the response's claim. This is unusually strong corroboration for an eval grading task — the assistant's grounding claims check out completely against live re-verification, not just self-report in notes.md.

notes.md is candid about a real but unflagged gap: imaging-ml-skill's reference guides (pyradiomics_guide.md, model_selection.md, notebook_templates.md, environment_setup.md) are 0 bytes/empty, which will block Section 3 (feature/model selection) once intake completes. The assistant chose not to surface this to the researcher in response.md, reasoning it isn't yet operative at the routing/intake stage. This is a defensible judgment call but worth noting as a transparency tradeoff: a more conservative response might have proactively flagged that the next phase has a known blocker, especially since this is a 'worst case' routing eval scenario.

The claim 'cmb_mel ... is listed as linked to "Clinical" supporting data in IDC's collection metadata (meaning the imaging is intended to pair with the CTDC clinical record, not duplicate it)' is plausible and consistent with general IDC/CTDC CMB design (matching patient ID prefix MSB-##### was independently confirmed), but I did not independently verify the specific 'linked to Clinical' metadata flag in IDC's collections_index (my idc-index version exposed a differently-named attribute and I did not chase down the exact field). This single sub-claim is the only one in the response not independently re-confirmed in this grading pass; everything else checked out byte-for-byte.

The response correctly distinguishes CTDC-linked melanoma imaging (cmb_mel) from CTDC-unlinked melanoma imaging+genomics collections (tcga_skcm, tcga_uvm, cptac_cm), correctly noting these would NOT pair with CTDC clinical data the same way — this is an important and accurate routing nuance that prevents a plausible researcher mistake (assuming any melanoma IDC collection pairs with CTDC).

The response appropriately declines to fully enumerate all 11 melanoma-matching IDC collections found by the live query, naming only 3 as examples and not claiming exhaustiveness in the response text — consistent with notes.md's self-report and avoids implying false completeness.

Overall this is a strong example of compliant 'ground, don't fabricate' behavior: the worst-case routing/cohort-size scenario produced a response that gives a number, but the number is real, reproducible, hedged with appropriate caveats (anonymous-tier undercounting, snapshot-in-time, modality-dependent usable cohort being much smaller than 42), and is explicitly subordinated to follow-up intake questions before any analysis plan or notebook is generated.
